summary: IS-IS floods link state information within an area or a domain, but some uses need other scopes. This document defines new PDUs that provide additional flooding scopes and extra space for information.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS spreads routing information by flooding it, sending copies to every router in a defined area or subdomain until they all have the same copy. This RFC adds new kinds of flooding, so the same reliable mechanism can be used for a smaller group of routers or for a larger one, and it adds a way of publishing far more information from a single router.

subtitle: New IS-IS packets that flood link state data to scopes beyond an area or the Level 2 subdomain, with room for far more of it.

tldr.problem: IS-IS floods link state information to every router in an area, and to every router in the Level 2 subdomain. Some deployments need information to reach a smaller set, such as the routers on one circuit, and some need a single router to publish more link state than the standard 256 packets allow.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new packet types, an FS-LSP, an FS-CSNP and an FS-PSNP, that reuse the existing Update Process but carry a scope number in place of the Maximum Area Addresses field. It also defines extended TLVs with 16-bit type and length fields, so a single object can be described in more than 255 octets.
tldr.outcome: Information can be flooded reliably to a chosen scope, such as one circuit or a whole domain, and a router can publish 64 K additional link state packets at each level. The new packet types are not understood by older routers, so every router in the scope has to be upgraded before the scope is used.

today: RFC 7356 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the three new IS-IS packet types, the scope identifier registry and the Scope Flooding Support TLV, and it is the extension that lets IS-IS flood outside the area and Level 2 subdomain.

sections.title: Why New Flooding Scopes
sections.content:
The Update Process, as defined by IS-IS, provides reliable and efficient flooding of information to all the routers in a given flooding scope. Currently the protocol supports two flooding scopes and the associated packets. Level 1 link state packets are flooded to all the routers in an area, and Level 2 packets are flooded to all the routers in the Level 2 subdomain.

The basic operation of the Update Process can be applied to any subset of the routers in a given topology, so long as that topology is not partitioned. It is therefore possible to introduce new packets in support of other flooding scopes and use the same Update Process machinery to provide the same reliability and efficiency it currently provides for the Level 1 and Level 2 scopes. The RFC defines these new packets and the modified Update Process rules to be used in supporting new flooding scopes.

New deployment cases have introduced the need for reliable and efficient circuit scope flooding. Appointed Forwarder information, as defined in RFC 7176, for example, needs to be flooded reliably and efficiently to all the Routing Bridges on a broadcast circuit. Currently only IS-IS Hellos have the matching scope, and those are unreliable, in that individual Hellos may be lost without affecting correct operation of the protocol. Providing reliability in cases where the set of information to be flooded exceeds the carrying capacity of a single packet requires sending the information periodically even when nothing has changed. When the information content is large this is inefficient and still gives no guarantee of reliability, so the RFC defines circuit scope flooding as a solution.

Another existing limitation is the carrying capacity of an LSP set. As noted in RFC 5311, the set of LSPs a system may originate at each level is limited to 256, and the maximum size of each is limited by the smallest Maximum Transmission Unit of any link used to flood them. That document defines a backwards-compatible extension to overcome the limitation if needed, but to stay interoperable with routers that do not support it, it restricts what can be advertised in the Extended LSPs and requires a router to be given several unique system IDs. A more flexible solution is possible where interoperability with legacy routers is not required. By definition, the introduction of new packets is not interoperable with legacy routers, so an alternative solution to the limited LSP set carrying capacity of Level 1 and Level 2 LSPs can be introduced at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage:
IS-IS works by flooding: every router sends its link state information to its neighbours, which forward it onwards, until the whole area has the same picture. The set of routers that receive it is the flooding scope, and IS-IS has two built in.

Two new needs have appeared. Sometimes the information should reach only the routers on one circuit, for example the Routing Bridges on a shared broadcast segment. The only IS-IS message with that reach is the Hello, and Hellos are allowed to be lost. The other need is more space: a router can publish only 256 link state packets at each level, and the workaround in RFC 5311 costs it several system IDs.

This RFC defines new packets that reuse the existing flooding machinery, so reach and reliability are the operator's to choose.

sections.title: Extended TLVs
sections.content:
Standard IS-IS TLVs, and the standard sub-TLVs first introduced in RFC 5305, have an 8-bit type field and an 8-bit length field. This constrains the information in a single TLV or sub-TLV to 255 octets. With the increasing use of sub-TLVs, it becomes more likely that the information about a single object that has to be advertised exceeds 255 octets, and in that case the information is encoded in multiple TLVs. That is less efficient, because the information that identifies the object has to be repeated in each TLV, and it adds implementation complexity on the receiving side, which must ensure that all the information about the object has been collected from the multiple TLVs.

The RFC therefore introduces extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs, encoded with a 16-bit type field and a 16-bit length field. Six restrictions apply to their use. They are permitted only in Flooding Scope packets that have a flooding scope designated for their use. A given flooding scope supports either the standard TLVs and sub-TLVs or the extended ones, but not both. Extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs MUST be used together, so standard sub-TLVs inside an extended TLV, or extended sub-TLVs inside a standard TLV, are invalid. If further levels of TLVs are introduced in future, the size of the type and length fields in those new sub-types MUST match the size used in the parent. The 16-bit fields are encoded in network byte order. And their use does not alter in any way the maximum size of packet that may be sent or received.

Standard TLV and sub-TLV code points from the IANA IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry MAY be used in extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs. The encoding is as specified for each of them, with three differences: the 8-bit type field is encoded as an unsigned 16-bit integer whose 8 most significant bits are all zero, the 8-bit length field is replaced by the 16-bit length field, and the length may take values greater than 255.
sections.plainLanguage:
The information IS-IS carries is organised into type-length-value fields, and each one has a type number and a length that are each one byte long. That caps the contents of a single field at 255 bytes. When one object needs more description than that, the description is split across several fields, and the identifying part has to be repeated in each one, which wastes space and complicates the receiving code.

The extended form simply doubles the type and length fields to two bytes each, so one field can carry much more. The rules are strict: a scope uses either the short form or the long form, never a mixture, and the long form may only appear in the new flooding packets.

sections.title: The Three New Packet Types
sections.content:
Three new packets are required to support the new flooding scopes: Flooding Scope LSPs, Flooding Scope Complete Sequence Number packets, and Flooding Scope Partial Sequence Number packets. Each is intentionally defined with a header as similar in format as possible to the corresponding packet type currently defined in IS-IS. Although it might have been possible to eliminate or redefine header fields in a new way, the existing formats are retained so that implementations can reuse as much of their existing packet processing logic as possible.

In all three, the Maximum Area Addresses field in the header of the corresponding standard packet has been replaced with a Scope field, so the maximum area address checks of IS-IS are not performed on these packets.

The FS-LSP carries the usual fixed header, with a PDU type of 10, followed by the FS LSP ID, which holds the system ID of the source in one of two formats: the standard format, with a source ID, a pseudonode ID and an FS LSP Number; or the extended format, with a source ID and a two-octet Extended FS LSP Number. Which format is used is specific to the scope and MUST be defined when that scope is defined. It then carries a sequence number, a checksum over the contents from the Source ID onwards, a byte whose bits hold the overload flag and the type of the Intermediate System, and the variable-length fields, which are specific to the scope.

The scope field holds seven bits of scope plus a priority bit. The value 0 is reserved and MUST NOT be used, and received FS-LSPs with a scope of 0 MUST be ignored and MUST NOT be flooded. If the priority bit is set, the LSP SHOULD be flooded at high priority. Scopes 1 to 63 are reserved for use with standard TLVs and standard sub-TLVs, and scopes 64 to 127 for use with extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs.

The FS-CSNP has a PDU type of 11 and, besides the fixed header, carries the source ID, the FS LSP ID of the first FS-LSP with the specified scope in the range covered by the packet, and the FS LSP ID of the last one. The FS-PSNP has a PDU type of 12 and carries the source ID. Its scope field also has an unsupported bit, where a value of 1 means the specified flooding scope is unsupported, and in that case no variable-length field other than authentication may be included in the packet.
sections.plainLanguage:
Three new kinds of packet are needed, and they deliberately look almost identical to the packets they sit alongside, so that the code which handles those can be reused. The one visible change is in the header: the field that says which area the packet belongs to is replaced by a field that says which flooding scope it belongs to.

Each carries the scope in seven bits, with one bit left over. In the link state packet that spare bit means flood this one at high priority, and in the partial sequence number packet it means this scope is not supported here.

The link state packet also carries an identifier for itself in one of two shapes. The short shape holds a one-byte number, the long one a two-byte number, which is what lets a router publish far more of them.

sections.title: Running the Update Process for a New Scope
sections.content:
The Update Process maintains a Link State Database for each level it supports. Each level-specific database holds the full set of LSPs generated by all the routers operating in that level-specific scope. The introduction of FS-LSPs creates an additional database for each additional scope supported, holding the FS-LSPs generated by the routers operating in that scope. There is therefore an additional instance of the Update Process for each supported flooding scope.

Operation of the scope-specific Update Process follows the Update Process specification in IS-IS. The circuits on which FS-LSPs are flooded are limited to those circuits participating in the given scope, and the sending and receiving of FS-CSNPs and FS-PSNPs is limited to the circuits participating in that scope. Consistent support of a given flooding scope on a circuit by all the routers operating on that circuit is required.

On a point-to-point circuit, when a new adjacency is formed, the synchronisation of all the FS databases supported on that circuit is required, so FS-CSNPs for all supported scopes MUST be sent when the new adjacency reaches the UP state, and the Send Receive Message bit MUST be set for all the FS-LSPs associated with the scopes supported on that circuit. Receipt of an FS-PSNP with the unsupported bit equal to 1 indicates that the neighbour does not support that scope, although it does support the new packets, and this MUST cause the Send Receive Message bit to be cleared for all the FS-LSPs with the matching scope that are currently marked for flooding on that circuit.

On a broadcast circuit, the new packets are sent to the same destination addresses as the standard packets for the given protocol instance. The Designated Intermediate System has the responsibility to generate periodic scope-specific FS-CSNPs for all supported scopes. A scope-specific Designated Intermediate System is NOT elected, because all the routers on a circuit must support a consistent set of flooding scopes. It is possible for a scope to be defined that is not level specific, in which case the Designated Intermediate System for each level enabled on the circuit must independently send the new packets for that scope to the appropriate level-specific destination address, which may result in redundant flooding.

Authentication TLVs MAY be included in the new packets. When authentication is in use, the scope is used first to select the applicable authentication configuration, and the authentication check is then performed as normal; scope-specific authentication MAY be used, but sharing authentication among several scopes and with the standard packets is considered sufficient. When the extended identifier format is used, the set of LSPs generated by a router may be large, so the priority bit may be used to identify those that hold information of higher priority, and such LSPs SHOULD be flooded at a higher priority than those without it. When an LSP is purged, the original state of the priority bit MUST be preserved.
sections.plainLanguage:
Every scope gets its own copy of the flooding machinery, its own database and its own set of rules, and the rules are the existing ones with the scope substituted for the level.

On a point-to-point link, the two routers synchronise their databases as soon as the link comes up, which means sending the summary packets for every scope the link supports. If the far end says it does not support one of the scopes, the near end stops trying to flood that scope on the link.

On a broadcast segment, the designated router takes responsibility for the periodic summary packets, and it is not elected for a scope, because every router on the segment has to agree on which scopes are in use.

sections.title: The Scopes That Are Defined
sections.content:
A flooding scope may be limited to a single circuit, which is a circuit scope, and circuit scopes may be further limited by level, giving a Level 1 Circuit Scope and a Level 2 Circuit Scope. A scope may be limited to all the circuits enabled for Level 1 routing, which is an area scope, or to all the circuits enabled for Level 2 routing, which is the Level 2 subdomain scope. Additional scopes may be defined that include all the circuits enabled for either Level 1 or Level 2 routing, which is a domain scope.

The RFC defines four circuit scope flooding identifiers: Level 1 Circuit Scope, which uses standard TLVs and standard sub-TLVs; Level 2 Circuit Scope, on the same basis; Extended Level 1 Circuit Scope, which uses extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs; and Extended Level 2 Circuit Scope, on the extended basis. FS-LSPs with the scope field set to one of these values contain information specific to the circuit on which they are flooded, and when received they MUST NOT be flooded on any other circuit. The extended identifier format is used in these packets. The database associated with circuit scope FS-LSPs consists of the set of FS-LSPs that both have matching circuit scopes and are transmitted locally or received on a specific circuit. The set of TLVs that may be included in such packets is specific to the use case and outside the scope of the document.

The RFC also uses the new packets to extend the LSP set capacity. When legacy interoperability is not a requirement, the use of FS-LSPs meets the need articulated in RFC 5311 without requiring alias system IDs to be assigned to a router. Four flooding scopes are defined for this purpose: Level 1 Flooding Scope and Level 2 Flooding Scope, using standard TLVs, and Extended Level 1 Flooding Scope and Extended Level 2 Flooding Scope, using extended TLVs. The Level 1 pair is flooded on all Level 1 circuits and the Level 2 pair on all Level 2 circuits. The extended identifier format is used in these packets, which provides 64 K of additional LSPs that may be generated by a single system at each level. These packets are used by the level-specific Decision Process in the same manner as standard LSPs, as additional information sourced by the same router, subject to three restrictions: a valid version of the standard LSP number 0 from the same router at the corresponding level MUST be present in the database for the set to be usable; information in an extended LSP that supports using the originating router as a transit node MUST NOT be used when the overload bit is set in the corresponding standard LSP number 0; and TLVs restricted to the standard LSP number 0 MUST NOT appear.

Domain scope flooding addresses the need to flood information throughout a domain, that is, to Level 1 routers in all areas as well as to routers in the Level 2 subdomain. Existing support for this uses leaking procedures between levels, which is sufficient when the data being flooded consists of individual TLVs. If it is desired to retain the identity of the originating router for the complete contents of a packet, then support for flooding the unchanged packet is desirable, and the RFC therefore defines two scopes for domain flooding: Domain Flooding Scope, using standard TLVs, and Extended Domain Flooding Scope, using extended TLVs. These packets MUST be flooded on all circuits regardless of what levels are supported on that circuit.

Using information in a domain scope FS-LSP depends on determining the reachability of the router that originated it, and no single router has the full view of the topology across all areas. The originator must therefore advertise an identifier that lets a receiving router decide whether the source is currently reachable. When IS-IS is deployed in support of Layer 3 routing for IPv4 or IPv6, the domain scoped FS-LSP number 0 MUST include at least one of the IPv4 Traffic Engineering Router ID, TLV 134, or the IPv6 Traffic Engineering Router ID, TLV 140. When IS-IS is deployed for Layer 2 routing, current standards support only a single area, so domain scope is not yet applicable.
sections.plainLanguage:
Four kinds of scope are defined, and each comes in two versions: one that uses the short type and length fields and one that uses the long ones. The version with the long fields has a scope number between 64 and 127.

A circuit scope reaches only the routers on one segment, and information sent in it never leaves that segment. A level scope reaches every router at that level, and it is what lets a router publish far more link state packets than the standard 256, because each packet's identifier has two bytes instead of one.

A domain scope reaches everything, across all the areas and the Level 2 part. The catch is that no single router knows the whole topology, so the originator has to include an identifier that lets the receivers work out whether it is still reachable.

sections.title: Deployment and Announcing Support
sections.content:
The introduction of new packet types is incompatible with legacy implementations. Legacy implementations do not support the scope-specific Update Process, so flooding of the FS-LSPs throughout the defined scope is unreliable when not all the routers in the scope support the new packets, and legacy implementations will likely treat the receipt of one of the new packets as an error. Even when all the routers in a given scope support the new packets, if not all the routers in the flooding domain for that scope support the scope itself, flooding may be compromised. Correct operation therefore requires that both the new packets and the new scope be supported by all the routers in the flooding domain of the new scope.

The unsupported bit in the FS-PSNP provides a means to suppress retransmissions of unsupported scopes. Routers that support the new packets SHOULD support sending an FS-PSNP with the unsupported bit equal to 1 when an FS-LSP is received with an unsupported scope, and SHOULD trigger management notifications when the new packets are received for unsupported scopes and when an FS-PSNP with the unsupported bit equal to 1 is received.

Announcements of support for a flooding scope may be useful in validating that full support has been deployed, and in isolating the reasons for incomplete flooding of FS-LSPs for a given scope. Routers supporting the new packets MAY announce the supported scopes in the Hello packets, using a new TLV called Scope Flooding Support, of type 243 and length 1 to 127, whose value is a list of supported scopes, one octet each. In a point-to-point Hello, the Level 1, Level 2, domain and all circuit scopes may be advertised. In a Level 1 LAN Hello, the Level 1, domain and Level 1 circuit scopes may be advertised, and the Level 2 scopes MUST NOT be. In a Level 2 LAN Hello, the Level 2, domain and Level 2 circuit scopes may be advertised, and the Level 1 scopes MUST NOT be. Information in this TLV MUST NOT be considered in adjacency formation, and whether it is used to decide when FS-LSPs of a locally supported scope are flooded is an implementation choice.
sections.plainLanguage:
The new packets are not understood by older routers, and an older router will probably treat receiving one as an error. So every router that has to be reached by a new scope has to be running the new code before that scope is used, and not only the routers in the scope itself but the whole flooding domain around it.

Two mechanisms help an operator find out what is wrong. A router that receives a packet for a scope it does not support can send back a message saying so, which stops the sender repeating the flood. And each router can list the scopes it supports in its Hello packets, so an operator can compare the lists and see where the gaps are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security concerns for IS-IS are addressed in IS-IS itself, in RFC 5304 and in RFC 5310. The new packets introduced are subject to the same security issues as their standard counterparts, and to the extent that the additional packets represent additional load for the routers in the network, they increase the opportunity for denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The new packets carry the same kind of information and are authenticated in the same way as the packets they replace, so they carry the same risks. The one extra risk is that there are more of them, and more traffic to flood is more traffic for an attacker to aim at.

items.label: FS-LSP
items.desc: The flooding scope link state packet, carrying the information to be flooded.

items.label: FS-CSNP
items.desc: The flooding scope complete sequence number packet, used to summarise and to request the whole range of packets in a scope.

items.label: FS-PSNP
items.desc: The flooding scope partial sequence number packet, used to request specific packets and to say that a scope is not supported.

viz.caption: THE SCOPE IDENTIFIERS THIS RFC DEFINES
THE FOUR KINDS OF FLOODING SCOPE

items.title: Circuit scope
items.text: Limited to the routers on a single circuit, and further limited by level. Information in it is never flooded on any other circuit.

items.title: Area scope
items.text: Limited to all the circuits enabled for Level 1 routing.

items.title: Level 2 subdomain scope
items.text: Limited to all the circuits enabled for Level 2 routing.

items.title: Domain scope
items.text: Includes all the circuits enabled for either Level 1 or Level 2 routing, so it crosses every area of the domain.
